\chapter{Small Creatures}
\label{ch:te-small-creatures}
\hlchaptermodality{70}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five small Telugu creatures and answer yes or no about them.}

Complete TE-C70-spider and demonstrate the chapter promise.

\section[eluka]{\te{ఎలుక} (eluka) — a mouse, a rat}

\label{lesson:TE-C70-mouse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{karra} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{ఎలుక}}
\textbf{\te{ఎలుక}} (\emph{eluka}) — \textquotedblleft{}a mouse, a rat\textquotedblright{}.

\te{ఎలుక} is a mouse, and the same word does for a rat. Telugu does not split them the way English does; when the size matters, a word for size is added.

It is inherited. Any house with \te{బియ్యం} in it has an \te{ఎలుక} story, and the \te{పిల్లి} you already know earns its keep here.

Asked whether there is one about, most people say \te{అవును} before they have thought about it, and \te{లేదు} only after going to look.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One. And the first thing anybody asks about a house.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{eluka}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{eluka}, then \emph{avunu}, then \emph{lēdu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{ఎలుక} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a mouse, a rat\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kappa]{\te{కప్ప} (kappa) — a frog}

\label{lesson:TE-C70-frog}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{eluka} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{కప్ప}}
\textbf{\te{కప్ప}} (\emph{kappa}) — \textquotedblleft{}a frog\textquotedblright{}.

\te{కప్ప} is a frog. Set it beside \te{కప్పు}, the roof, and you have a pair worth saying twice: one small vowel at the end is the whole difference.

It is inherited and it belongs to the rains. The first \te{కప్ప} heard after dark is how a \te{గ్రామం} knows the season turned, before anybody looks at a calendar.

Telugu uses it for somebody whose world is small — a \te{కప్ప} in a well, which is a picture a dozen unrelated languages reached for on their own.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two. And the roof is still \te{కప్పు}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kappa}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kappu}, then \emph{kappa}, and say which one is the roof
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{కప్ప} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a frog\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dōma]{\te{దోమ} (dōma) — a mosquito}

\label{lesson:TE-C70-mosquito}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kappa} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{దోమ}}
\textbf{\te{దోమ}} (\emph{dōma}) — \textquotedblleft{}a mosquito\textquotedblright{}.

\te{దోమ} is a mosquito. The word is inherited, and it is said with feeling.

A \te{దోమ} is the reason for the net over a bed, for smoke at dusk, and for half the complaints of a hot \te{సాయంత్రం}.

It is also the standard small annoyance. Somebody waving away a threat calls it a \te{దోమ}, and somebody who could not sleep blames one.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three. The smallest of them and the loudest complaint.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dōma}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{dōma}, then \emph{kappa}, and say which one you hear at night
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{దోమ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a mosquito\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[uḍuta]{\te{ఉడుత} (uḍuta) — a squirrel}

\label{lesson:TE-C70-squirrel}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{dōma} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{ఉడుత}}
\textbf{\te{ఉడుత}} (\emph{uḍuta}) — \textquotedblleft{}a squirrel\textquotedblright{}.

\te{ఉడుత} is a squirrel — the striped palm squirrel that runs along the top of a \te{గోడ} and out onto any \te{కొమ్మ} it can reach.

It is inherited. The three stripes down its back carry a story that every Telugu household can tell, and the animal is let alone because of it.

An \te{ఉడుత}'s help is a set phrase for a small contribution offered honestly. Whoever says it is calling their own share tiny and means to give it anyway.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four. The one nobody chases off.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{uḍuta}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{uḍuta}, then \emph{eluka}, and say which one is welcome
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{ఉడుత} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a squirrel\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sālīḍu]{\te{సాలీడు} (sālīḍu) — a spider}

\label{lesson:TE-C70-spider}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{uḍuta} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{సాలీడు}}
\textbf{\te{సాలీడు}} (\emph{sālīḍu}) — \textquotedblleft{}a spider\textquotedblright{}.

\te{సాలీడు} is a spider — the one in the corner where the \te{గోడ} meets the \te{కప్పు}.

It is inherited, and it is built on the old Telugu word for a weaver, so the name says what the creature does. The thread a person works with is \te{దారం}, which you already have.

Ask whether one has been swept out and the answer is a plain \te{అవును} or \te{లేదు}, which is where five small creatures have got you.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \te{ఎలుక}, \te{కప్ప}, \te{దోమ}, \te{ఉడుత}, \te{సాలీడు}. Everything small enough to share a house with.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sālīḍu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then \emph{avunu} for the ones in your house and \emph{lēdu} for the rest
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{సాలీడు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a spider\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
